title: The 10 Best Cordless Heat Guns
subtitle: Battery-powered heat guns ranked from live Amazon data: shrink tubing, vinyl, and quick heat jobs away from an outlet.
intro: A cordless heat gun runs on the same battery pack as your drill, which makes it the tool for shrink tubing on a truck, a frozen fitting in a crawlspace, or vinyl trim on a ladder. The best-sellers are mostly bare tools for DEWALT, Milwaukee, RYOBI, CRAFTSMAN, and Makita packs, plus cheaper 350-watt guns built to fit those batteries. We ranked 10 on rating, review volume, and features (adjustable temperature, included nozzles, a work light, and whether a battery comes in the box).

changelog.note: Page published with 10 ranked picks and 1 tool to avoid.

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX Heat Gun Kit, Cordless, Up to 990 Degrees, 42 Minutes of Run Time, LED Light, Battery and Charger Included (DCE530P1)

Lock-on button for long passes and a lock-off trigger

$158.18 is a lot if you only shrink tubing now and then

avoid.name: Performance Tool W2082 Compact Rechargeable Cordless Heat Gun, 600 Degree Max Output
avoid.verdict: A 3.6-volt pocket heater sold as a heat gun. It tops out at 600°F, runs 15 to 20 minutes, and the battery is built in, so it can't strip paint or thaw a pipe and it's finished when the cell wears out.
reasons: Its maximum is 600°F. Every pick on this page reaches at least 875°F, and paint, adhesive, and frozen-pipe work need that range.
The 3.6 V, 2.0Ah battery is built in. You can't swap in a fresh pack mid-job, and when the cell wears out the tool is done.
The listing gives 15 to 20 minutes of work per charge, then up to 2 hours to recharge over USB.
The listing contradicts itself on weight: the bullets say 4.8 ounces, the spec table says 8 ounces.
At 3.5 stars it's the lowest-rated gun we considered for this page.

buyers_guide.q: Is a cordless heat gun as strong as a corded one?
buyers_guide.a: No. A corded heat gun draws 1,200 to 2,000 watts from the wall; the third-party battery guns here are rated at 350 watts, and battery packs can't sustain corded-level output for long. Cordless guns are for shrink tubing, small vinyl and plastic jobs, and spots with no outlet. For stripping a door or a window frame, see our corded heat gun ranking.

buyers_guide.q: How long does a battery last?
buyers_guide.a: Shorter than you'd guess. DEWALT lists up to 42 minutes for the DCE530, CRAFTSMAN up to 15 minutes, and Makita 21 minutes on high with a 6.0Ah pack. The 350-watt third-party guns list about 6 minutes on a 2.0Ah pack and about 12 on a 4.0Ah. Use the largest battery you own, and keep a second one charged for longer jobs.

buyers_guide.q: Should I buy the brand-name gun or a battery-compatible one?
buyers_guide.a: If you use it often, buy the gun from the company that makes your batteries: it's built for that pack, and DEWALT, Milwaukee, RYOBI, CRAFTSMAN, and Makita back their own tools. The compatible guns from LIVOWALNY and Edtran cost a third to a half as much and add adjustable heat, which makes them reasonable for occasional shrink-tube and craft work. Their makers don't share a warranty with the battery brand.

For vinyl wrap, thin plastic, and anything that scorches, yes. The DEWALT, Milwaukee, RYOBI, and CRAFTSMAN listings give a single maximum temperature, from 875 to 990°F, with no low setting. The Makita has variable temperature, and the third-party guns have two settings or a digital range.

A reflector wraps heat around shrink tubing and pipe, a concentrator or reduction nozzle focuses it on a small spot, a flat or wide-slot nozzle spreads it along a strip of paint or adhesive, and a glass protector keeps heat off window panes. The Milwaukee 2688-20 is the only gun here that ships without one.

buyers_guide.q: Is it safe to leave the battery on?
buyers_guide.a: Take it off when you're done. The LIVOWALNY listings warn that the gun drains the battery if it's left attached. Set the gun down on a non-flammable surface until the nozzle cools; it stays hot after you release the trigger.
